headline: Facebook counted anger as five likes
dek: In 2018 Mark Zuckerberg retuned Facebook's feed to favor posts people talked about.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Stop checking every page
slides.text: On early Facebook, seeing what friends were up to meant visiting their profiles one by one. On September 5, 2006, Facebook launched News Feed, which gathered friends' updates in one place.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: A billion people a month
slides.text: Users protested at first: one group against it drew more than 700,000 members in days. Then the feed became the heart of the site. By October 2012 more than a billion people used Facebook each month. In June 2026, 3.6 billion a day used Meta's apps.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: A fix for passive scrolling
slides.text: In January 2018 Zuckerberg changed the feed's goal from relevant content to "meaningful social interactions," citing people's well-being. Posts likely to spark comments and replies would rank higher. He said he expected time spent on Facebook to fall.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Comments, or arguments
slides.statLabel: points for a "significant" comment against 1 for a like in Facebook's 2018 feed scoring, internal documents show
slides.text: Facebook's researchers found publishers and political parties tilting their posts toward outrage, which drew comments. They also wrote that "misinformation, toxicity, and violent content are inordinately prevalent among reshares."
also: Sources: internal documents reported by CNN, the Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post, 2021. Facebook says the formula is continually refined.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Still argued over
slides.text: Facebook's own researchers flagged the effect by 2019. Outside, the science is contested: a 2023 study run with Meta found a chronological feed didn't measurably change polarization in three months. Critics said Meta's election measures muddied that.

slides.label: The cleanup
slides.title: Turning down the dial
slides.text: In late 2020 Facebook cut the weight of an angry reaction to zero. From 2021 it put less weight on how likely people are to comment on or share political posts. Zuckerberg called the claim that it pushes angry content for profit "deeply illogical."

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: 3.6 billion people a day on Meta's apps, June 2026
Friends' news in one place, free to use, since 2006
Ranked feeds showed less untrustworthy and political content than a plain timeline (Science, 2023)
costs: Publishers and parties tilting posts toward outrage, Facebook's researchers found (WSJ, 2021)
On Facebook, the ranked feed showed more uncivil posts and slurs than a plain timeline (same study)
An angry reaction once counted five times a like (Washington Post, 2021)
slides.text: The feed keeps billions of people in touch. By its makers' own research, it also favored outrage in politics and news. How much that changed society is still argued over. You decide.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: Credit where it's due
slides.text: Zuckerberg took on a real problem: keeping up with the people you care about. In 2018 he chose a goal he said would cost time on the site. His company also opened data to outside researchers studying the 2020 election, which is part of why we know this much.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: Replies can't tell you why
slides.text: The feed counted comments and reshares as signs of meaningful talk. An angry post earns comments too. The number went up whether people were connecting or fighting, so the ranking couldn't tell the two apart.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your numbers drift too
slides.text: You judge your newsletter by its open rate. Subject lines get punchier, then a little alarming. Opens go up. So do unsubscribes, and readers start skimming past you. The number you chased stopped meaning what you wanted.
also: A sales team paid per call, not per sale
Support tickets closed fast, then reopened

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: A number stands in for a goal only until people learn what moves the number.
A count of replies can't tell a good conversation from a fight.
Inside research often spots a problem early. What happens next is a separate decision.
